title: Example: find the hidden file
writeup:
## 🎯 Goal

Create a folder on your own machine with a hidden file inside, then find it again using only the command line.

## 🔍 Process

1. `mkdir -p ~/practice/hidden-demo && cd ~/practice/hidden-demo`
2. `echo "found me" > .secret.txt`
3. Run `ls` (nothing shown) and then `ls -a`.
4. Search from the parent folder: `find ~/practice -name ".secret*"`.

## 💥 Solution

`ls -a` shows names that start with a dot; `find` searches by name whether or not it is hidden.

## 🧠 What I learned

(your notes here)

## 🛠️ Commands Used

`ls`, `cd`, `find`, `cat`

title: Example: who failed to log in?
writeup:
## 🎯 Goal

Practise log triage with a pipeline. Make a small fake log first so nothing real is involved.

## 🔍 Process

1. Create `auth.log` with a few lines such as `Failed password for admin from 198.51.100.7`, `Accepted password for alice from 192.0.2.4`, repeated with different users and addresses.
2. Keep only failures: `grep "Failed" auth.log`.
3. Extract the address: `awk '{print $NF}'` (or `cut` if your lines have a fixed shape).
4. Rank them: `... | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`.

## 💥 Solution

`grep "Failed password" auth.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`

## 🧠 What I learned

(your notes here)

## 🛠️ Commands Used

`grep`, `awk`, `sort`, `uniq`

title: Example: scan my own machine
writeup:
## 🎯 Goal

See your own computer the way a scanner does, and compare it with what the operating system says is listening. Only scan machines you own.

## 🔍 Process

1. List listening sockets: `ss -tulpn` (Linux) or `lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -n -P` (macOS).
2. Scan yourself: `nmap -sV -p- 127.0.0.1`.
3. Start something to find: `python3 -m http.server 8000` in another terminal, then scan again.
4. Confirm one port with `nc -zv 127.0.0.1 8000`.

## 💥 Solution

The new port 8000 appears in both views. Anything nmap sees that you did not expect deserves a look.

## 🧠 What I learned

(your notes here)

## 🛠️ Commands Used

`ss`, `nmap`, `nc`
